title: Sensory Processes: Attention and Perception
summary: Sensation is the process by which one form of energy (e.g. light) is converted into neural impulses by stimulation of sensory neurons, resulting in awareness of conditions inside or outside the body. Absolute threshold is the minimum physical energy needed to produce a sensory experience; difference threshold is the minimal change between two stimuli that can be recognised. Background and expectation affect sensation (stars invisible by day; you hear the doorbell of an expected friend).

The five senses: sight (light waves, eye), hearing (sound waves, ear), skin senses (touch, cold, warmth, pain), smell (olfaction; nose; volatile materials) and taste (gustation; tongue; soluble materials). Vision: the eye works like a camera; Newton showed white light splits into the visible spectrum; colour blindness is partial or total inability to distinguish colours. Hearing: sound needs a medium (not travelling in vacuum); pitch depends on frequency (Hz), loudness on amplitude (decibels), timbre on the complexity of the wave. Vestibular sense: bodily orientation with respect to gravity. Kinesthetic sense: position and movement of body parts. Taste: four primary qualities – sweet, sour, bitter, saline – with receptors in taste buds. Skin: sensitivity to pressure is highest on face, tongue and hands. Pain: response to noxious stimuli; affected by psycho-social and cultural factors.

Perception is the process of organising and interpreting sensations into meaningful patterns; the brain selects, organises and integrates information. Some perceptions are inborn and many are learnt. The physical object is the distal stimulus; the image on the retina is the proximal stimulus; the task of perception is to infer the distal from the proximal stimulus. Stages: sensory stimulation, synthesis of features, analysis, identification and recognition with the help of expectations, beliefs and knowledge.

Figure–ground organisation: sensations are grouped into objects (figures) standing out against a background; the reversible goblet shows figure–ground reversal. Laws of grouping: proximity (nearby stimuli grouped), similarity (similar size, shape, colour), continuity (dotted circle seen as a circle), closure (completing an incomplete figure) and common region. Perceptual constancy: perception of size, shape and brightness stays the same although the retinal image changes (size, shape and brightness constancy). Depth perception: ability to see three-dimensional space and judge distance, partly innate and partly learnt; monocular cues (one eye; pictorial cues like converging railway tracks) and binocular cues (retinal disparity). Illusions are distorted perception of existing stimuli (Müller-Lyer, Ponzo, horizontal–vertical); hallucination is perception with no external reality.

Attention is focusing the senses on a particular stimulus. Selective attention gives priority to one sensory message; divided attention (driving while using a phone) can cause accidents. Functions: sensory filter, response selection, gateway to consciousness. Determinants: physical factors (repetition, contrast, size, shape, brightness, packaging) and motives (a hungry person notices food words; advertisers use anxiety and desire to be attractive).

ESP is perceiving objects or events in ways not explained by known senses; parapsychology studies psi-phenomena: clairvoyance (perceiving events unaffected by distance or barriers), telepathy (reading another's thoughts), pre-cognition (predicting future events) and psycho-kinesis (influencing objects by will). Most psychologists do not accept ESP. Applications: eyewitness testimony is prone to errors, especially under stress; habituation is ceasing to attend to repeated familiar stimuli, and creative people keep attending; breaking perceptual habits and paying attention gives better results.

sa: Absolute threshold is the minimum physical energy needed to produce a sensory experience; difference threshold is the minimal change in two stimuli that can be recognised, e.g. noticing a change in TV volume.
Describe pitch, loudness and timbre of sound.
Pitch is highness or lowness determined by frequency (Hz). Loudness is physical intensity determined by amplitude, measured in decibels. Timbre is the quality due to the complexity of the sound wave.

Perception of an object's size, shape or brightness remains the same although its retinal image changes: a distant person appears the same size (size constancy), a tilted door appears rectangular (shape constancy), and paper appears equally white in different lighting (brightness constancy).
Distinguish monocular and binocular cues of depth.

Monocular cues work with one eye and include pictorial cues like converging railway tracks. Binocular cues need two eyes and arise from retinal disparity, the difference in the images of the two eyes; a one-eyed person has limited depth perception.

Physical factors – repetition, contrast, size, shape and brightness – attract attention (packaging and advertising). Motives also direct attention: a hungry person notices food; advertisers use anxiety and the desire to be attractive.
Describe the problem with eyewitness testimony.
Eyewitness errors in perception are common, especially when the person is surprised, stressed or threatened; hence investigators and jurors should gather more evidence than rely only on eyewitnesses.
la: Define perception and discuss the principles of perceptual organisation.

Perception is the process of organising and interpreting sensations into meaningful percepts using past and present experience. Perception is organised: figure–ground organisation separates objects from the background, and grouping follows proximity, similarity, continuity, closure and common region. Perceptual constancy and depth perception further stabilise the world.
Discuss depth perception and perceptual constancy.

Depth perception is the ability to see three dimensions and judge distance; it is partly innate and partly learnt. Monocular and binocular cues (retinal disparity) provide it; pictorial cues such as converging tracks also help. Perceptual constancy keeps size, shape and brightness stable despite changing retinal images. Illusions such as Müller-Lyer show distortion.
Explain the senses and their stimuli and organs.

Sight: light waves, eye; hearing: sound waves, ear; skin senses: touch, cold, warmth and pain; smell: volatile materials, nose; taste: soluble materials, tongue with four primary tastes. In addition there are vestibular (orientation) and kinesthetic (movement) senses. Thresholds determine what we detect.
What is extra-sensory perception? Describe its types and the applications of perception in daily life.

ESP is perception not explained by known senses: telepathy, clairvoyance, pre-cognition and psycho-kinesis, studied by parapsychology; most psychologists doubt it. Applications: eyewitness testimony is error-prone; habituation reduces attention to familiar stimuli while creative people continue to attend; paying attention and breaking perceptual habits improve results.
